title: Day 9X — I2C: Two Wires, and a Display That Works

slides.title: Where we are
items: Today we'll start communicating with the seven-segment display in your kit.
This is a new peripheral, and we'll communicate with it using a new protocol.
We'll continue going to the reference manual for register information.
We'll start by wiring the display to two of the Nucleo's pins, flashing a program, and making sure the display lights up.
Everything after that answers the question you then have: how was that possible with just two wires?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min with announcements. 50-minute session — say the shape out loud, because the payoff lands early today rather than late.

How Did Two Wires Do That?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 5 min. NOTHING WAS ASSIGNED TO READ, so this is taught from scratch. The side-by-side against UART, then the two consequences of sharing that the comparison does not cover.

slides.presenterNote: ≈ 8 min. The message first, field by field, then the one rule that makes START and STOP unmistakable, then they find all of it on their own screen. Nothing was assigned to read, so build it — do not open on "as you saw".

Reading Your Own Trace
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min. Debrief together. The decode view is the first thing to cut if the clock is tight — it is a second route in, not new material.

slides.title: The transaction your loop is producing
The Number on the Wire
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 4 min. They already have the answer on their screens and do not know it yet: the byte they read off the address phase is 0xE0 and their program says 0x70. Let the activity land before the reveal. Keep it short — the point is that the library shifts, not a tour of address formats.

slides.title: Which number is on the wire?
The address phase, read off the trace
0x70 is seven bits. The wire carries eight
Write One Digit Yourself
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 10 min. CRUCIAL, second half: every student has derived a segment byte and put it on a digit of their own choosing. Nobody leaves without this — if the clock is tight, drop the four-letter word and keep tasks 1 to 4.

slides.title: The segment names, and the bit order
Put your own character on a digit
Recap
items: Two wires, shared by everything on them: a clock the controller drives, and a data line every device can pull LOW and none can drive HIGH.
A transaction is START, seven address bits, the R/W bit, an ACK from whoever recognized the address, data bytes each with their own ACK, and a STOP. You have one on a screen with your name on it.
A digit's byte is 0b DP g f e d c b a, and the display buffer is two bytes per position: digits at 0, 2, 6 and 8, the colon at 4.
Leave the display wired, since tomorrow starts by flashing helloDisplay.c again.
